title: Arguing a position
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A structured case is a SHAPE OF TALK and not a piece of grammar, and this module is the cheapest of the level because the ladder already bought every part of it. prathamam, tataḥ, anantaram and ante enumerate (L2-M10); yataḥ gives the reason and ataḥ draws the conclusion (L1-M9); avaśyam with kintu concedes and holds (L4-M4, L1-M10); mama mate marks the position (L4-M4). The spend here is three words and one verb cell.

dvitīyam and tṛtīyam continue L2-M10's prathamam and are built the same way: a neuter word standing as an adverb, taking no ending and never agreeing with anything. They head their own sentence, as prathamam does, and they count POINTS rather than objects — 'second,' and 'third,' and not 'two things' or 'the third book'.

uttaram is the answer as a THING, neuter — something an argument HAS. uttaram asti is 'there is an answer', and a claim is made into one with L3-M5's iti: <claim> iti atra uttaram. It is not L2-M3's uttamam, 'excellent', which is one letter away and a different word entirely.

vadet is the optative of L2-M7's vadati — the stem with -et, exactly as L3-M4 built gacchet, khādet and paṭhet. A pre-empted objection is a HYPOTHETICAL utterance, so it takes the mood L4-M5 already named as this course's hedge: avaśyam samayaḥ na asti iti bhavān vadet is 'you might of course say there is no time'.

THE OBJECTION IS RAISED IMPERSONALLY AND NOT BY 'SOMEBODY'. The indefinite pronoun is written nowhere on this course: every dictionary prints it joined, with external sandhi and an avagraha, and undoing the join gives two words whose rows say 'who' and 'also' — a learner tapping for 'someone' would be told neither. So an objection is atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, which costs nothing, or it is put in bhavān's mouth with vadet.

English marks the shape of an argument with paragraphs and with the voice, and under-marks it in words. Sanskrit signposts on the SURFACE: without the ordinals and without ataḥ, three claims in a row are a pile of assertions and not a case. Say the number out loud — prathamam, dvitīyam, tṛtīyam — where English would only pause.

English 'so' is a consequence word AND a filler you say while thinking. ataḥ may only head a CONSEQUENCE — never a cause, never a pause. If what follows is the reason rather than the result, the word is yataḥ, and the two are not interchangeable in either language.

The concession machinery is L4-M4's and is reused untouched: avaśyam grants the point IN ADVANCE and kintu takes the turn, while tathāpi grants the fact and denies the consequence you expected from it. A case that concedes nothing is heard as a case that has not listened.

mama mate opens a position and does not weaken it. It is not a hedge — L4-M5's prāyaḥ and L3-M3's kadācit are the hedges — and it does not ask for agreement. Put it at the front, say the claim, and give the reason with yataḥ.

STILL WRITTEN NOWHERE, and named here because this is the module that would otherwise reach for them. Every optative cell beyond the seven L3-M4 and L4-M3 opened and this module's vadet: no dual, no plural, no second singular, and not the athematic kuryāt, which L3-M4 refused and L4-M3 refused again. -anīya is named at L4-M1 and is still written nowhere.

sentences.display: mama mate pratidinam adhyayanam hitam asti.
sentences.cue: In my opinion, daily study is beneficial.
sentences.literal: of-me in-opinion every-day study good is

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion, and the whole idiom is two words that never change shape.
L4-M4's 'in opinion' shape. mama mate opens a position; it marks the claim as yours and does not soften it.
L1-M4's 'daily'. It takes no ending, and here it narrows the claim: the case is about a habit and not about one afternoon.
L3-M2's studying, as a noun. It is what this whole module argues about, and it is neuter, so hitam beside it ends -am.
L4-M4's 'good for somebody', as against L2-M3's uttamam, which simply praises. It is the word an argument holds its ground with.
L1-M3's copula, optional in a sentence like this one and written here because the claim is being stated rather than assumed.

sentences.trap: mama mate is not a hedge. English 'in my opinion' often apologises for the claim behind it; this does not, and a Sanskrit case that wants softening reaches for prāyaḥ or kadācit instead.
sentences.sound: MA-ma MA-tay pra-ti-DI-nam a-dhya-YA-nam HI-tam AS-ti. The dhy of adhyayanam is one aspirated d followed by y, said in one beat. At speed mate pratidinam runs together with no pause at all.

variations.display: mama mate pratidinam adhyayanam hitam.
variations.cue: In my opinion, daily study is beneficial.
variations.changed: the copula falls away, which it always may: a nominal sentence was already complete
variations.script: मम मते प्रतिदिनम् अध्ययनम् हितम्।

variations.display: bhavataḥ mate pratidinam adhyayanam hitam asti.
variations.cue: In your opinion, daily study is beneficial.
variations.changed: the position is handed to the listener, and only the owner of the opinion moves
variations.script: भवतः मते प्रतिदिनम् अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति।

variations.display: kim bhavataḥ mate pratidinam adhyayanam hitam asti?
variations.cue: In your opinion, is daily study beneficial?
variations.changed: asked rather than asserted, which is how a case invites the other side in
variations.script: किम् भवतः मते प्रतिदिनम् अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति?

sentences.usage: The opening move of a case: say whose view it is, say the claim, and stop. Everything after this sentence is support for it, and a listener who hears mama mate knows that support is coming.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the view before you defend it.
sentences.script: मम मते प्रतिदिनम् अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति।

mistake.display: mama mate pratidinam adhyayanam hitaḥ asti.
mistake.why: hitam is neuter because adhyayanam is. hitaḥ would agree with a masculine noun, and there is none in the line — an adjective copies the gender of the word it sits on and never of the speaker.

words.note: L2-M10's first sequencer, opening a numbered point rather than an event. It sits at the very front and takes no ending.
The subject here. A neuter noun looks the same whether it acts or is acted on, so word order and the verb do the sorting.
L5-M3's knowledge, neuter, and the thing given. It is what a case for studying claims first, because it is the least arguable half.
L5-M1's 'gives'. An abstract noun can be the giver here exactly as vidyā is in vidyā dadāti vinayam.

sentences.trap: prathamam counts the POINT and not the time. It does not mean the studying happens first; it means this is the first thing being said in favour of it.

variations.display: prathamam adhyayanam jñānam dadāti, tataḥ vinayam dadāti.
variations.cue: First, study gives knowledge; then it gives good conduct.
variations.changed: a second clause is hung off the first with L2-M10's tataḥ, which orders the giving rather than the points
variations.script: प्रथमम् अध्ययनम् ज्ञानम् ददाति, ततः विनयम् ददाति।

variations.display: prathamam vidyā jñānam dadāti.
variations.cue: First, learning gives knowledge.
variations.changed: the subject forks to L5-M1's vidyā, and nothing else in the sentence moves
variations.script: प्रथमम् विद्या ज्ञानम् ददाति।

variations.display: kim adhyayanam jñānam dadāti?
variations.cue: Does study give knowledge?
variations.changed: the point is turned into the question it answers, which is how an objector would put it
variations.script: किम् अध्ययनम् ज्ञानम् ददाति?

sentences.usage: The first support. Keep each numbered point to one short sentence: the ordinal is doing the work of a paragraph break, and a long sentence behind it buries the number.

words.note: 'Second', the neuter standing as an adverb — the same shape and the same job as L2-M10's prathamam. It never agrees with anything and never bends.
L5-M1's learning, feminine, and the subject of the saying this point quotes. It is the vidyā already inside L1-M6's vidyālayaḥ.
L5-M1's good conduct, the object here. This point is M1's subhāṣita used as evidence rather than recited.
'Gives'. The whole clause is the first quarter of a well-known saying, which is why it is worth borrowing for a case.

sentences.trap: dvitīyam is not the ordinary word for 'two'. L1-M8's dve counts things; dvitīyam ranks them, and only one of the two can head a point in an argument.

variations.display: anantaram vidyā vinayam dadāti.
variations.cue: After that, learning gives good conduct.
variations.changed: the ordinal is swapped for a sequencer, which orders the points in time instead of numbering them
variations.script: अनन्तरम् विद्या विनयम् ददाति।

variations.display: dvitīyam adhyayanam vinayam dadāti.
variations.cue: Second, study gives good conduct.
variations.changed: the subject moves back to the module's own noun, so the point stops leaning on the saying
variations.script: द्वितीयम् अध्ययनम् विनयम् ददाति।

variations.display: kim vidyā vinayam dadāti?
variations.cue: Does learning give good conduct?
variations.changed: the claim in the form an objector would put it, which is the version worth having an answer to
variations.script: किम् विद्या विनयम् ददाति?

sentences.usage: Borrowing a saying as a point is normal and effective: the listener has heard the line before, so the point lands before it is argued. Quote the pāda and stop — the rest of the verse is not needed here.

mistake.why: The ordinal is an ADVERB here and is fixed at dvitīyam. Made to agree with vidyā it stops numbering the point and starts describing the learning — 'the second learning gives good conduct'.

sentences.cue: Third, study is an excellent habit.

words.note: 'Third', built like dvitīyam and prathamam. Its first vowel is the ṛ of L2-M3's kṛṣṇaḥ, a vowel and not a consonant plus i.
The subject, neuter. What it is SAID TO BE keeps its own gender, which is why the two words after it end -aḥ.
L2-M3's warm praise. It agrees with abhyāsaḥ, the word it describes, and not with the neuter subject in front of it.
L4-M8's habit, masculine. A predicate noun keeps its own gender, so a neuter subject may be called a masculine thing without anything bending.
L1-M3's copula, written here because the line has two nouns in it and the reader needs to know which one is the predicate.

sentences.trap: uttamaḥ ends -aḥ and the subject is neuter. That is not an error: an adjective agrees with the noun it sits on, and here it sits on abhyāsaḥ, which is masculine.
sentences.sound: tri-TEE-yam a-dhya-YA-nam ut-ta-MAH a-BHYAA-sah AS-ti. The ṛ of tṛtīyam is a vowel: a short r said as the whole middle of the syllable, with no a or i around it.

variations.display: tṛtīyam adhyayanam uttamaḥ abhyāsaḥ.
variations.cue: Third, study is an excellent habit.
variations.changed: the copula drops, leaving the bare nominal sentence this language prefers
variations.script: तृतीयम् अध्ययनम् उत्तमः अभ्यासः।

variations.display: ante adhyayanam uttamaḥ abhyāsaḥ asti.
variations.cue: Finally, study is an excellent habit.
variations.changed: the last point is marked as last with L2-M10's closer instead of with a number
variations.script: अन्ते अध्ययनम् उत्तमः अभ्यासः अस्ति।

variations.display: adhyayanam uttamaḥ abhyāsaḥ na asti iti kaḥ vadet?
variations.cue: Who would say that study is not an excellent habit?
variations.changed: negated and asked at once, with the new optative carrying a question nobody is expected to answer
variations.script: अध्ययनम् उत्तमः अभ्यासः न अस्ति इति कः वदेत्?

sentences.usage: Three points is the shape a case takes here, and three is usually enough. A fourth is heard as padding unless it is the one that answers the objection.

sentences.display: yadi adhyayanam na asti, tarhi jñānam api na asti.
sentences.cue: If there is no study, then there is no knowledge either.
sentences.literal: if study not is, then knowledge also not is

words.note: L3-M4's 'if', opening its clause where English puts it. The clause it opens is complete on its own and comes first.
L1-M2's 'not', standing in front of the verb. na asti is fixed: the copula may be dropped when positive and never when denied.
L3-M4's 'then', opening the consequence. Unlike L3-M2's correlatives it may be left out without breaking the sentence.
L5-M3's knowledge. It is what the first point claimed study gives, denied here by denying its cause.
L1-M10's 'also', standing AFTER the word it adds to. jñānam api is 'knowledge too' and never 'also knowledge'.

sentences.trap: The conditional is doing the work of evidence here, not of a hedge. L4-M5's optative doubts a claim; yadi … tarhi asserts a link between two facts and is as firm as the case gets.

variations.display: yadi adhyayanam asti, tarhi jñānam api asti.
variations.cue: If there is study, then there is knowledge too.
variations.changed: the negation is lifted from both halves, which is the same claim said from the other side
variations.script: यदि अध्ययनम् अस्ति, तर्हि ज्ञानम् अपि अस्ति।

variations.display: yadi adhyayanam na asti, tarhi vinayam api na asti.
variations.cue: If there is no study, then there is no good conduct either.
variations.changed: the consequence forks to the second point, showing that one condition can carry both
variations.script: यदि अध्ययनम् न अस्ति, तर्हि विनयम् अपि न अस्ति।

variations.display: adhyayanam na asti, ataḥ jñānam api na asti.
variations.cue: There is no study, so there is no knowledge either.
variations.changed: the condition becomes a fact and the link becomes a consequence, which is ataḥ's only job
variations.script: अध्ययनम् न अस्ति, अतः ज्ञानम् अपि न अस्ति।

sentences.usage: The cheapest evidence a case can offer: deny the cause and watch the effect go with it. It is honest only when the link really is that tight, and a listener will say so when it is not.
sentences.script: यदि अध्ययनम् न अस्ति, तर्हि ज्ञानम् अपि न अस्ति।

sentences.display: avaśyam samayaḥ na asti iti bhavān vadet.
sentences.cue: Of course, you might say there is no time.
sentences.literal: certainly time not is quote your-honour might-say

words.note: L4-M4's concession, granting the point IN ADVANCE. It is what makes the kintu behind it a turn instead of a contradiction.
L4-M7's time, masculine — time to spend rather than a reading on a clock. It is the objection every case about a habit meets.
L3-M5's quotative, closing the objection. It carries a whole sentence into this one as a single thing said.
L1-M2's polite 'you'. The objection is put in the listener's mouth, and the verb stays third person as it always does beside this word.
The optative of L2-M7's vadati — the stem with -et, as L3-M4 built gacchet and paṭhet. It is a row of its own here, pointing back at vadati.

sentences.trap: vadet is not a request and not a command. L2-M7's vadatu asks somebody to speak; vadet says only that they MIGHT speak, which is exactly what a pre-empted objection needs.
sentences.sound: a-VASH-yam SA-ma-yah NA AS-ti I-ti bha-VAAN va-DAYT. The -et of vadet is one long e and the t is dental — the tongue on the teeth, not behind them.

mistake.display: avaśyam samayaḥ na asti iti bhavān vadatu.
mistake.why: vadatu asks the listener to say it. The sentence then invites the objection instead of answering it before it is made, and the whole move is lost. The hypothetical takes vadet.

variations.display: avaśyam bhavān evam vadet.
variations.cue: Of course, you might say so.
variations.changed: the objection is pointed at rather than quoted, with L5-M3's evam standing in for the whole of it
variations.script: अवश्यम् भवान् एवम् वदेत्।

variations.display: avaśyam samayaḥ na asti iti bhavatī vadet.
variations.cue: Of course, you might say there is no time.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, and only the address word moves: the verb never agreed with her
variations.script: अवश्यम् समयः न अस्ति इति भवती वदेत्।

variations.display: samayaḥ na asti iti kadācit bhavān vadet.
variations.cue: You might perhaps say there is no time.
variations.changed: the concession is dropped and a hedge put in its place, which weakens the move rather than softening it
variations.script: समयः न अस्ति इति कदाचित् भवान् वदेत्।

sentences.usage: The strongest thing a case can do is say the objection first, in the other person's voice, and better than they would. avaśyam grants it, vadet keeps it hypothetical, and the answer comes next.
sentences.mnemonic: Say their line before they do.
sentences.script: अवश्यम् समयः न अस्ति इति भवान् वदेत्।

sentences.display: alpam api adhyayanam hitam asti iti atra uttaram.
sentences.cue: The answer here is that even a little study is beneficial.
sentences.literal: a-little also study good is quote here answer

words.note: L2-M9's 'a little'. With api behind it, it is 'even a little' — the smallest amount that still counts, which is what an answer to a time objection needs.
The module's subject again, narrowed by alpam api. The claim is deliberately smaller than S01's and is therefore harder to argue with.
L3-M5's quotative, turning the whole claim into the one thing the answer consists of.
L1-M7's 'here', pointing at this place in the argument rather than at a place in a room. It takes no ending and never will.
The answer as a thing, neuter. It is NOT L2-M3's uttamam, 'excellent': one letter apart and nothing in common.

sentences.trap: The answer narrows the claim rather than repeating it. S01 argued for daily study; this answers the time objection by asking for less, and a case that refuses to narrow anything is heard as one that cannot.

variations.display: atra uttaram idam.
variations.cue: Here is the answer.
variations.changed: the claim is dropped and only the frame is left, which is what a speaker says before pausing
variations.script: अत्र उत्तरम् इदम्।

variations.display: alpam api adhyayanam hitam asti.
variations.cue: Even a little study is beneficial.
variations.changed: the frame falls away and the claim stands alone, which is the same sentence outside an argument
variations.script: अल्पम् अपि अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति।

variations.display: kim alpam api adhyayanam hitam asti?
variations.cue: Is even a little study beneficial?
variations.changed: the answer is put back as a question, which is the objector's next move rather than the speaker's
variations.script: किम् अल्पम् अपि अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति?

sentences.usage: How an answer is framed: the claim, then iti, then atra uttaram. Saying atra uttaram first and the claim after is also heard, and the module's variation shows it, but the claim-first order is the commoner one.
sentences.script: अल्पम् अपि अध्ययनम् हितम् अस्ति इति अत्र उत्तरम्।

mistake.display: alpam api adhyayanam hitam asti atra uttaram.
mistake.why: Without iti the claim and the frame collide: the line has two verbless halves and nothing joining them. iti is what turns a whole claim into the one thing an answer consists of.

sentences.display: atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, tathāpi uttaram asti.
sentences.cue: There is one question here; even so, there is an answer.
sentences.literal: here one question is, even-so answer is

words.note: L1-M8's 'one', masculine here because praśnaḥ is. It is doing the work English gives to 'a' — there is no article in this language.
L5-M5's question as a thing. atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti is how an objection is raised when nobody is named as raising it.
L1-M10's 'even so', opening its sentence. It grants the fact before it and then denies the consequence you expected from it.
The answer, neuter, in the same shape as when it is the object: a neuter noun keeps one shape whether it acts or is acted on.

sentences.trap: Nobody asks this question. There is no word for 'someone' anywhere on this course, and the impersonal frame is not a workaround — it is what a speaker says, and it keeps the objection from being pinned on the listener.

variations.display: atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti.
variations.cue: There is one question here.
variations.changed: the objection is raised and left standing, which is what a listener does rather than a speaker
variations.script: अत्र एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति।

variations.display: atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, kintu uttaram api asti.
variations.cue: There is one question here, but there is an answer too.
variations.changed: tathāpi gives way to kintu, which turns rather than concedes, and api adds the answer instead of insisting on it
variations.script: अत्र एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति, किन्तु उत्तरम् अपि अस्ति।

variations.display: atra ekaḥ saṃśayaḥ asti, tathāpi uttaram asti.
variations.cue: There is one doubt here; even so, there is an answer.
variations.changed: a doubt in place of a question, which is L4-M5's word and admits more than this one does
variations.script: अत्र एकः संशयः अस्ति, तथापि उत्तरम् अस्ति।

sentences.usage: Raise the hardest objection yourself, impersonally, and answer it in the same breath. A case that leaves its own weak point for the other side to find has handed them the turn.
sentences.mnemonic: One question, one answer, one sentence.
sentences.script: अत्र एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति, तथापि उत्तरम् अस्ति।

sentences.display: pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ asti, ataḥ adhyayanam kartavyam.
sentences.cue: The result is excellent, so study should be done.
sentences.literal: result excellent is, so study must-be-done

words.note: L4-M2's result. It is a row of its own because phalam, the other Sanskrit word for a result, means fruit on this course and nothing else.
L2-M3's praise, ending -aḥ to agree with the masculine noun in front of it.
L1-M9's 'so', at the FRONT of the consequence. It may never head a cause — that is yataḥ — and it is never a pause.
L4-M1's gerundive of karoti, fixed neuter -am. It agrees with nothing and names nobody, which is why a conclusion can use it.

sentences.trap: kartavyam names no one who must do it. L4-M1 taught it with mayā or bhavatā beside it; a conclusion leaves that out on purpose, so the obligation falls on whoever is listening.

variations.display: pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ asti, ataḥ adhyayanam kartavyam iti manye.
variations.cue: The result is excellent, so I think study should be done.
variations.changed: the conclusion is handed back to the speaker with L3-M3's manye, which softens the obligation
variations.script: परिणामः उत्तमः अस्ति, अतः अध्ययनम् कर्तव्यम् इति मन्ये।

variations.display: pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ na asti, tathāpi adhyayanam kartavyam.
variations.cue: The result is not excellent; even so, study should be done.
variations.changed: the premise is denied and the conclusion held, which is what tathāpi is for
variations.script: परिणामः उत्तमः न अस्ति, तथापि अध्ययनम् कर्तव्यम्।

variations.display: kim pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ asti?
variations.cue: Is the result excellent?
variations.changed: the premise alone, asked — the one question that could bring the whole conclusion down
variations.script: किम् परिणामः उत्तमः अस्ति?

sentences.usage: The conclusion of a case: a premise everybody now accepts, ataḥ, and the thing that follows. Say it once. Repeating a conclusion is heard as doubting it.
sentences.script: परिणामः उत्तमः अस्ति, अतः अध्ययनम् कर्तव्यम्।

mistake.display: pariṇāmaḥ uttamaḥ asti, yataḥ adhyayanam kartavyam.
mistake.why: yataḥ heads a REASON and ataḥ heads a RESULT. Swapped, the sentence says study should be done because the result is excellent — which reverses the direction of the argument the module just built.

sentences.display: ante adhyayanam eva varam iti aham manye.
sentences.cue: In the end I think study itself is better.
sentences.literal: in-the-end study indeed better quote I think

words.note: L2-M10's closer. It tells a listener the case is finishing, and nothing else in an argument does that job.
L5-M1's emphasiser, standing AFTER the word it lifts. adhyayanam eva is 'study itself'; put it in front and it lifts nothing.
L2-M9's 'better'. It never changes shape for what it describes, so it sits beside a neuter subject without bending.
L1-M1's 'I'. It is written here because the closing claim is being owned, not because manye needs it.

words.cue: I think · I am of the view
words.note: L3-M3's 'I think', ending -e like L1-M1's rocate. It closes the case by naming whose case it was.

sentences.trap: manye at the end is not a retreat. It returns the claim to the speaker after the argument has been made, which is a different move from mama mate at the start — that announced a position, this signs it.
sentences.sound: AN-tay a-dhya-YA-nam AY-va VA-ram I-ti a-HAM MAN-yay. eva is one long e and never two syllables; manye ends in a short e that is still fully sounded.

variations.display: adhyayanam eva varam iti aham manye.
variations.cue: I think study itself is better.
variations.changed: the closer drops away and the sentence stops being the end of anything
variations.script: अध्ययनम् एव वरम् इति अहम् मन्ये।

variations.display: ante adhyayanam eva varam iti mama matam.
variations.cue: In the end, my view is that study itself is better.
variations.changed: the verb gives way to the noun, which is the heavier and more written-sounding of the two
variations.script: अन्ते अध्ययनम् एव वरम् इति मम मतम्।

variations.display: ante vidyā eva varam iti aham manye.
variations.cue: In the end I think learning itself is better.
variations.changed: the closing claim widens from the activity to the thing it produces
variations.script: अन्ते विद्या एव वरम् इति अहम् मन्ये।

sentences.usage: Close by naming the view again and owning it. A case that ends on its last piece of evidence sounds unfinished; ante and manye together are the full stop.
sentences.mnemonic: End where you began, and sign it.
sentences.script: अन्ते अध्ययनम् एव वरम् इति अहम् मन्ये।

comprehensionPool.cue: In my opinion this is excellent.

comprehensionPool.display: atra ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, kintu bhayam na asti.
comprehensionPool.cue: There is one question here, but there is nothing to fear.
comprehensionPool.script: अत्र एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति, किन्तु भयम् न अस्ति।

comprehensionPool.display: avaśyam bhavān evam vadet, kintu aham na manye.
comprehensionPool.cue: Of course you might say so, but I do not think it.
comprehensionPool.script: अवश्यम् भवान् एवम् वदेत्, किन्तु अहम् न मन्ये।

comprehensionPool.display: atra bhavataḥ praśnaḥ asti, uttaram api asti.
comprehensionPool.cue: Your question is here, and there is an answer too.
comprehensionPool.script: अत्र भवतः प्रश्नः अस्ति, उत्तरम् अपि अस्ति।

comprehensionPool.cue: So study should be done every day.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi samayaḥ asti, tarhi adhyayanam kartavyam.
comprehensionPool.cue: If there is time, then study should be done.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि समयः अस्ति, तर्हि अध्ययनम् कर्तव्यम्।

comprehensionPool.cue: In the end there is only one answer.
In my opinion the result is excellent.

comprehensionPool.display: avaśyam idam satyam, tathāpi mama matam bhinnam.
comprehensionPool.cue: Certainly this is true; even so, my view is different.
comprehensionPool.script: अवश्यम् इदम् सत्यम्, तथापि मम मतम् भिन्नम्।
